name: Big Data Computing & Business Analytics
desc: Analytical architecture, Hadoop, MapReduce, SparkContext, RDDs, analytics lifecycle, association & sequence rules, graph analytics, social network metrics

topics.name: Big Data & Typical Analytical Architecture
notes: **Big Data Vs**: **Volume, Velocity, Variety** (+ Veracity, Value). Data types: structured, semi-structured (JSON, XML), unstructured (text, images, video).

**Typical analytical architecture**: data sources → ingestion (Kafka, Flume, Sqoop) → storage (**HDFS / data lake**, data warehouse) → **processing & analytics (Hadoop MapReduce, Spark)** → serving (OLAP, NoSQL) → **BI tools for dashboards and reports** (Tableau, Power BI).
**Data lake** = raw data in native format (schema-on-read). **Data warehouse** = cleaned, structured, integrated data for analysis (schema-on-write).
**OLAP = Online Analytical Processing** (complex analytical queries on historical, multidimensional data; operations: roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice, pivot). **OLTP** = day-to-day transactions.
**Columnar databases** store data column by column → **faster analytical queries** (read only the needed columns) and better compression.
Traditional EDW limits: data silos, slow ETL, expensive scaling → leads to analytic sandboxes and Hadoop-based platforms.

topics.name: Hadoop Framework, HDFS & YARN
notes: **Hadoop** = open-source framework for distributed storage (**HDFS**) and processing (**MapReduce**, on **YARN**) on commodity hardware. Key strengths: **high fault tolerance and scalability** (batch-oriented, not low-latency).
**HDFS = Hadoop Distributed File System**: files split into large **blocks (default 128 MB in Hadoop 2/3; 64 MB in Hadoop 1)**, each **replicated 3 times** by default across DataNodes (rack-aware).

**NameNode** (master) stores **metadata** (namespace, file → block → DataNode mapping). **DataNodes** store the actual blocks and send heartbeats. **Secondary NameNode** checkpoints metadata (fsimage + edit log) — it is NOT a hot backup.
**YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator)** manages and schedules cluster resources: **ResourceManager** (global), **NodeManager** (per node), **ApplicationMaster** (per job), containers.

Ecosystem: **Hive** (SQL-like HiveQL), **Pig** (Pig Latin dataflow scripts), **HBase** (column-oriented NoSQL, random real-time access), **Sqoop** (RDBMS ↔ HDFS), **Flume** (log ingestion), **Oozie** (workflow scheduling), **ZooKeeper** (coordination), Mahout (ML).
Data locality: move computation to where the data is.

topics.name: Batch Analysis with Hadoop MapReduce
notes: **MapReduce** = batch programming model: **Map** → (Combine) → **Shuffle & Sort** → **Reduce**.

**Mapper** maps input key/value pairs to a set of **intermediate key/value pairs** (transforms data into key-value form). **Map task** processes one input split (chunk). Number of map tasks = number of input splits.
**Reduce** consolidates/aggregates the results of all map tasks for each key. **Shuffle** moves map output to the right reducer (by the **partitioner**, usually hash of the key) and sorts it by key.
**Combiner** = a "mini-reducer" run on map output locally to reduce network traffic.
Word count: map emits (word, 1); reduce sums the counts per word.
MapReduce writes intermediate data to disk → good for large batch jobs, slower for iterative work (Spark keeps data in memory).

topics.name: Apache Spark & SparkContext
notes: **Spark** = fast, general, **in-memory** cluster computing engine (often 10–100× faster than MapReduce for iterative work). Components: Spark Core (RDDs), Spark SQL/DataFrames, Streaming, MLlib, GraphX.

**SparkContext** = the entry point of a Spark application (created in the **driver program**); it connects to the **cluster manager** (Standalone, YARN, Mesos, Kubernetes), which allocates **executors** — resources are allocated at the **executor level**. In Spark 2+, **SparkSession** wraps the SparkContext.
Key configuration: **spark.master** (cluster URL), spark.driver.memory, spark.executor.memory/cores, **spark.default.parallelism** (default number of partitions/parallelism for RDD operations).
**sc.setCheckpointDir(dir)** sets the directory where **checkpoint data** is stored (checkpointing truncates long lineages).

Execution: action → **DAG** of stages (split at shuffle boundaries) → tasks per partition. The DAG scheduler and Catalyst optimizer (SQL) **optimise the plan** (pipelining narrow transformations, choosing a physical plan).
**Data locality**: schedule tasks on nodes holding the data → less network overhead.

topics.name: Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs) & Creating RDDs
notes: **RDD** = immutable, partitioned, fault-tolerant collection processed in parallel. **Resilient** = rebuilt from **lineage** (the recorded chain of transformations) if a partition is lost — immutability makes lineage-based recovery possible.
**Creating RDDs**: (1) **sc.parallelize(collection)**, (2) from external storage — **sc.textFile("hdfs://…")**, (3) by **transforming an existing RDD**.

**Transformations** (lazy, return a new RDD): map, filter, flatMap, **reduceByKey**, groupByKey, join, union, distinct, sortByKey. **Actions** (trigger computation, return a result or write output): **count, collect**, take, first, reduce, **saveAsTextFile**, foreach.
**Lazy evaluation**: nothing runs until an **action** is called → Spark can optimise the whole chain.

**Narrow** transformations (map, filter) need no data movement. **Wide** transformations (reduceByKey, groupByKey, join) **shuffle** data across the cluster. reduceByKey is preferred over groupByKey (combines locally first).
**cache()/persist()** keep an RDD in memory — useful when the **RDD is reused/computed multiple times** (iterative algorithms). cache() = persist(MEMORY_ONLY).
Key advantage over HDFS-based processing: **in-memory data processing**.

topics.name: Data Analytics Lifecycle
notes: **Data Analytics Lifecycle** (EMC): **1. Discovery** (learn the domain, frame the problem, define **objectives, success criteria/KPIs**, form hypotheses) → **2. Data Preparation** (analytic sandbox, ETL/ELT, data conditioning — often the longest phase) → **3. Model Planning** (choose methods and variables) → **4. Model Building** (build and test models) → **5. Communicate Results** → **6. Operationalize** (deploy, pilot, monitor, **validate against real-world data and adjust**).
The process is **iterative** — you can move back to earlier phases.
Key roles: business user, project sponsor, project manager, BI analyst, DBA, data engineer, **data scientist**.
**KDD = Knowledge Discovery in Databases**: selection → preprocessing → transformation → **data mining** → interpretation/evaluation.
Unstructured-data challenges: **data integration and data quality** → address with **data governance and ETL processes** (+ appropriate storage like data lakes/NoSQL).
Mining tasks: **time series analysis** (attribute value as it varies over time), regression, classification, clustering, association rules, sequence discovery.

topics.name: Association Rules & Apriori
notes: **Support count** = frequency of occurrence of an itemset (number of transactions containing it). **Support** = support count / total transactions.
**Confidence(A → B)** = Support(A ∪ B) / Support(A) — i.e. P(B | A), where A ∪ B means the itemset containing both A and B.
**Lift(A → B)** = Confidence(A → B) / Support(B). Lift > 1 → positive association; = 1 → independent; < 1 → negative.
**Frequent itemset**: support ≥ minimum support threshold. **Strong rule**: meets min support AND min confidence.

**Apriori property (anti-monotone)**: every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent → if an itemset is infrequent, all its supersets are pruned. Apriori = generate candidates level by level (k-itemsets from frequent (k−1)-itemsets), prune, count.
Improving Apriori: **hash-based techniques**, **transaction reduction**, **partitioning**, **sampling**, dynamic itemset counting. **FP-Growth** avoids candidate generation using an FP-tree.
Classic market-basket example: {Diapers} → {Beer}.

topics.name: Sequence Rules & Sequential Pattern Mining
notes: **Sequential pattern mining** finds frequently occurring **ordered** sequences of events/itemsets (e.g. customers buy a laptop → then a laptop bag → then a mouse). **Order matters**, unlike plain association rules.
A **sequence** is an ordered list of itemsets (elements) ⟨{a}, {b, c}, {d}⟩. A sequence is contained in another if its elements appear in the same order (gaps allowed).
**Sequence support** = fraction of customer/data sequences that contain the pattern. A **sequence rule** X ⇒ Y means "Y tends to follow X".
Algorithms: **GSP** (Generalized Sequential Patterns — Apriori-based, level-wise), **SPADE** (vertical id-lists), **PrefixSpan** (pattern growth, projected databases).
Applications: web clickstreams, purchase histories, DNA, medical event sequences.
**Sequence discovery** is the data-mining task of finding such sequential patterns.

topics.name: Graph Analytics Techniques
notes: **Graph analytics** studies entities (vertices/nodes) and relationships (edges): social networks, fraud rings, recommendation, logistics, the web.

Techniques: **path analysis** (shortest paths — Dijkstra/BFS), **connectivity** (connected components, bridges), **centrality** (degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector, **PageRank**), **community detection** (Louvain, label propagation, modularity), **triangle counting**, link prediction, similarity.
**PageRank**: a page is important if important pages link to it; uses a damping factor (≈ 0.85) and iterates until convergence.
Tools: **Spark GraphX**, Pregel model (Google — vertex-centric **Bulk Synchronous Parallel** supersteps), Apache Giraph, **Neo4j** (graph DB, Cypher query language).
Representations: adjacency matrix (dense), adjacency list (sparse), edge list.

topics.name: Social Network Metrics
notes: **Degree centrality** = number of direct connections (normalised: degree / (n − 1)). High degree = popular/hub.
**Betweenness centrality** = how often a node lies on **shortest paths between other nodes** → brokers/bridges controlling information flow (the centre of a star has maximum betweenness).
**Closeness centrality** = 1 / (sum of shortest distances to all other nodes) (or (n − 1) / Σd) → how quickly a node can reach everyone.
**Eigenvector centrality** = connected to other well-connected nodes (PageRank is a variant).
**Network density** = actual edges / possible edges; undirected possible = n(n − 1)/2.
**Clustering coefficient** = fraction of a node's neighbour pairs that are connected (triangles) → "my friends are friends".

Other: **diameter** (longest shortest path), average path length, **homophily** (similar people connect), **bridges/structural holes**, reciprocity (directed), in-degree (popularity) vs out-degree (activity).
